# IANA-managed Reserved Domains

# IANA-managed Reserved Domains

Certain domains are set aside, and nominally registered to “IANA”, for specific policy or technical purposes.

## Example domains

As described in [RFC 2606](/go/rfc2606) and [RFC 6761](/go/rfc6761), a number of domains such as example.com and example.org are maintained for documentation purposes. These domains may be used as illustrative examples in documents without prior coordination with us. They are not available for registration or transfer.

## Test IDN top-level domains

These domains were temporarily delegated by IANA for the [IDN Evaluation](http://www.icann.org/topics/idn/) being conducted by [ICANN](http://www.icann.org/).

## Policy-reserved domains

We act as both the registrant and registrar for a select number of domains which have been reserved under policy grounds. These exclusions are typically indicated in either technical standards (RFC documents), or [contractual limitations](http://www.icann.org/en/registries/agreements.htm).

Domains which are described as registered to IANA or ICANN on policy grounds are not available for registration or transfer, with the exception of country-name.info domains. These domains are available for release by the ICANN Governmental Advisory Committee Secretariat.

## Other Special-Use Domains

There is additionally a [Special-Use Domain Names](/assignments/special-use-domain-names) registry documenting special-use domains designated by technical standards. For further information, see [Special-Use Domain Names](/go/rfc6761) (RFC 6761).

content.title: Headless browser - Wikipedia
content.markdown:
# Headless browser - Wikipedia

A headless browser is a [web browser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_browser) without a [graphical user interface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphical_user_interface).

Headless browsers provide automated control of a web page in an environment similar to popular web browsers, but they are executed via a [command-line interface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Command-line_interface) or using network communication. They are particularly useful for [testing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_testing) web pages as they are able to render and understand HTML the same way a browser would, including styling elements such as page layout, color, font selection and execution of [JavaScript](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JavaScript) and [Ajax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajax_(programming)) which are usually not available when using other testing methods.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Since version 59 of [Google Chrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Chrome)[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-:0-3) and version 56[[4]](#cite_note-4) of [Firefox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firefox),[[5]](#cite_note-5) there is native support for remote control of the browser. This made earlier efforts obsolete, notably [PhantomJS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PhantomJS).[[6]](#cite_note-6)

## Use cases

The main use cases for headless browsers are:

- [Test automation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Test_automation) in modern [web applications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_application) ([web testing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_testing))

- Taking screenshots of web pages.

- Running automated tests for JavaScript libraries.

- Automating interaction of web pages.

### Other uses

Headless browsers are also useful for [web scraping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_scraping). [Google](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google) stated in 2009 that using a headless browser could help their search engine index content from websites that use Ajax.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

Headless browsers have also been misused in various ways:

- Perform [DDoS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DDoS) attacks on web sites.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

- Increase advertisement impressions.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

- Automate web sites in unintended ways[[10]](#cite_note-10) e.g. for [credential stuffing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credential_stuffing).[[11]](#cite_note-11)

However, a study of browser traffic in 2018 found no preference by malicious actors for headless browsers.[[3]](#cite_note-:0-3) There is no indication that headless browsers are used more frequently than non-headless browsers for malicious purposes, like DDoS attacks, [SQL injections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SQL_injection) or [cross-site scripting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-site_scripting) attacks.

## Usage

As several major browsers natively support headless mode through [APIs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/API), some software exists to perform browser automation through a unified interface. These include:

- [Selenium WebDriver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selenium_(software)#Selenium_WebDriver) – a [W3C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W3C) compliant implementation of WebDriver[[12]](#cite_note-12)

- [Playwright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playwright_(software)) – a [Node.js](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node.js) library to automate Chromium, Firefox and WebKit[[13]](#cite_note-13)

- Puppeteer – a [Node.js](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node.js) library to automate Chrome or Firefox[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15)

### Test automation

Some [test automation software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Test_automation) and frameworks include headless browsers as part of their testing apparatus.[[3]](#cite_note-:0-3)

- [Capybara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capybara_(software)) uses headless browsing, either via [WebKit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebKit) or Headless Chrome to mimic user behavior in its testing protocols.[[16]](#cite_note-16)

- [Jasmine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jasmine_(JavaScript_testing_framework)) uses Selenium by default, but can use WebKit or Headless Chrome, to run browser tests.[[17]](#cite_note-17)

- [Cypress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cypress_(software)), a frontend testing framework

- [QF-Test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QF-Test), a software tool for automated testing of programs via the graphical user interface where a headless browser can also be used for testing.

### Alternatives

Another approach is to use software that provides browser APIs. For example, [Deno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deno_(software)) provides browser APIs as part of its design. For [Node.js](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node.js), jsdom[[18]](#cite_note-18) is the most complete provider. While most are able to support common browser features (HTML parsing, [cookies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP_cookie), [XHR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XMLHttpRequest), some JavaScript, etc.), they do not [render](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rendering_(computer_graphics)) the [DOM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Document_Object_Model) and have limited support for [DOM events](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DOM_events). They usually perform faster than full browsers, but are unable to correctly interpret many popular websites.[[19]](#cite_note-19)[[20]](#cite_note-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21)

Another is [HtmlUnit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HtmlUnit), a headless browser written in Java. HtmlUnit uses the [Rhino engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhino_(JavaScript_engine)) to provide JavaScript and Ajax support as well as partial rendering capability.[[22]](#cite_note-22)[[23]](#cite_note-23)
